pos: n. (Augustin Marlorat, 1506–1562, Huguenot pastor at Rouen, compiler of the New Testament catena, hanged for the gospel)
etymology: Latin Augustinus, venerable; French Marlorat, a surname of uncertain origin.
biblical_def: Augustin Marlorat was put into an Augustinian house as a boy, came to the gospel by reading, fled to Geneva, and was sent back into France as a pastor. He served at Paris and then at Rouen, where he was the leading minister when the city declared for the Reformed cause in 1562. He also produced one of the most used books of the age: a catena, or linked commentary, on the whole New Testament and on Isaiah and the Psalms, in which the comments of the fathers and the Reformers are set out under each verse so that a preacher could see the best that had been said. When the royal army retook Rouen in October 1562 Marlorat was arrested, tried, and hanged before his own church. The dictionary keeps the two things together. He had spent his life gathering the church's exposition of Scripture into one place for the use of other men, and he died in the street outside the building where he had preached it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines catena as a chain or connected series, and commentary as a series of comments or annotations.
webster_full: CATE'NA, n. A chain; a connected series, as a catena of authors or of comments.
COM'MENTARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; an exposition of a book.
AUGUS'TINIAN, n. One of an order of monks, so called from St. Augustine.
GIB'BET, n. A gallows; a post with an arm projecting, on which criminals are hanged.
scriptures: And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also.
These were more noble than those in Thessalonica, in that they received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: He compiled the fathers and Reformers on the whole New Testament, then was hanged outside his own church at Rouen.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern suspicion of a compiler, as though gathering what other men have said were a lesser labour than saying something new. Marlorat's catena served ten thousand sermons by preachers who could not own the libraries it digested, which is a plainer service to the church than most originality.

The principle to recover is that the church's exposition is a trust handed on, and that handing it on is pastoral work: “the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men” (2Ti 2:2). The use of such a book is Berean: so that a hearer may search “the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Act 17:11). And the end of such a man is seen under the fifth seal, among “the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9).

pos: n. (Jean de l'Espine, c. 1506–1597, Huguenot pastor at Angers and writer on the quiet of the Christian mind)
etymology: French Jean from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; de l'Espine, of the thorn.
biblical_def: Jean de l'Espine was an Augustinian who came out to the Reformed faith in middle life, pastored at Angers and elsewhere through the whole span of the French religious wars, and lived to be ninety. His best books are not polemics but treatises on the inward life: on the tranquillity of the mind, on patience in affliction, on the right use of the Lord's Supper, written for people whose churches were burned and whose relatives had been killed. The dictionary values that choice of subject. A pastor in a civil war is tempted to write only about the war. L'Espine wrote about how a Christian keeps a quiet mind when he has lost his property and buried his friends, and he wrote it as a man who had lived the question rather than as a man proposing a technique. The result is Reformed devotional writing of the first rank, and it is the opposite of what the therapeutic age means by self-care: the quiet he describes comes from outside the self, from God's decree and Christ's finished work, and not from managing one's feelings.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tranquillity as quietness and calmness of mind, and patience as the suffering of afflictions with a calm temper.
webster_full: TRANQUIL'LITY, n. Quietness; a calm state; freedom from disturbance or agitation of mind.
PA'TIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity or provocation with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
AFFLIC'TION, n. The state of being afflicted; a state of pain, distress or grief.
CONSOLA'TION, n. Comfort; alleviation of misery or distress of mind.
scriptures: Isa 26:3
Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee.
Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid.
Phi 4:7
And the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus.
Rom 5:3
And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience;
corruption_summary: He wrote on the quiet Christian mind for people whose churches were burned, and grounded it outside the self.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the therapeutic redefinition of peace. Modern self-help teaches that calm is a skill: regulate the feeling, reframe the thought, and the mind quiets itself. L'Espine, writing to congregations under arms, located peace somewhere no technique can reach — in the God who keeps the mind stayed on Him, and in a reconciliation already accomplished and not dependent on how the Christian happens to feel this week. The two accounts look similar from a distance and are opposite at the root: one makes the self the source of its own rest, the other receives rest as a gift.

The standard is the biblical one. “Thou wilt keep him in perfect peace, whose mind is stayed on thee: because he trusteth in thee” (Isa 26:3). The peace is Christ's own and is not the world's kind: “Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you” (Joh 14:27). It passes explanation and does the guarding itself — “the peace of God, which passeth all understanding, shall keep your hearts and minds through Christ Jesus” (Phi 4:7) — and tribulation is not its enemy but its school: “we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience” (Rom 5:3).

pos: n. (Jean Morel, d. 1574, Huguenot pastor and correspondent of Calvin)
etymology: French Jean from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Morel, from Old French more, dark, swarthy.
biblical_def: Jean Morel, lord of Collonges, was one of the pastors sent out of Geneva into the French churches in the years when those churches were being organised under persecution, and his correspondence with Calvin is part of the record of how that was done. The letters are not devotional: they are about where a minister can be placed, which congregation can pay, who has been arrested, whether a man of doubtful soundness should be received, how a church without a building should hold the Supper. The dictionary gives him an entry for the sake of that correspondence. The French Reformed church of the 1550s and 1560s was built by letter, under a government that would have hanged everyone named in them, and the men who wrote and carried those letters took the same risk as the men who preached. The ordinary administration of a persecuted church is one of the most unremembered forms of courage, and Morel's letters preserve its texture better than any martyrology.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines correspondence as intercourse by letters, and courier as a messenger sent in haste.
webster_full: CORRESPOND'ENCE, n. Intercourse between persons at a distance, by means of letters sent and answers received.
COU'RIER, n. A messenger sent express with letters or dispatches.
CLAN'DESTINE, a. Secret; private; hidden; withdrawn from public view.
ADMINISTRA'TION, n. The executive part of government; the management of any office or employment.
scriptures: Col 4:7
All my state shall Tychicus declare unto you, who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord:
Phm 1:12
Whom I have sent again: thou therefore receive him, that is, mine own bowels:
We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth.
Rom 16:3
Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus:
corruption_summary: His letters to Calvin are the working record of how a hunted church was organised and supplied with pastors.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a romance about the underground church that remembers only its heroics. The letters show the actual work: stipends, placements, bad candidates, arrests, and the slow business of getting a minister to a town that had asked for one. It was dangerous and it was clerical, and both words are true at once.

The principle to recover is that the New Testament is itself full of this traffic and names the men who carried it. Tychicus is sent so that the church may know Paul's state: “who is a beloved brother, and a faithful minister and fellowservant in the Lord” (Col 4:7). Onesimus is sent back by hand — “Whom I have sent again” (Phm 1:12). Those who receive and forward such messengers share in the work: “We therefore ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth” (3Jo 1:8). And the apostle names his fellow labourers one by one — “Greet Priscilla and Aquila my helpers in Christ Jesus” (Rom 16:3).

pos: n. (Jean Garnier, d. 1574, pastor of Geneva sent to serve the French churches)
etymology: French Jean from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Garnier, from Germanic Warinhari, guarding army.
biblical_def: Jean Garnier was one of the Genevan company of pastors in Calvin's and Beza's time, and like several of them he was spent on France. Geneva's register records a steady traffic of ministers examined, ordained and dispatched across the border to congregations that had asked for a preacher, knowing that a good proportion would be taken. Garnier served in that traffic and also in the Genevan pulpit and consistory. The dictionary names him for the system rather than for a single feat. Between 1555 and 1562 Geneva sent well over a hundred ministers into France, to churches that were illegal, in a kingdom that executed them; the city of some thirteen thousand souls functioned as a seminary and a staging post for a nation of millions. No committee planned it. A church that trains more ministers than it needs, and sends the surplus where they will probably die, is doing something the New Testament describes and the modern church rarely attempts.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines mission as a sending, and send as to cause to be conveyed or transmitted.
webster_full: MIS'SION, n. A sending or being sent, usually by authority, to perform some service; persons sent.
SEND, v.t. To cause to go or pass from one place to another; to commission to go and act.
CON'SISTORY, n. An assembly of ecclesiastical persons; the court of a bishop or a Reformed church session.
COM'PANY, n. An assemblage of persons; a band or body of persons associated for a common purpose.
scriptures: And how shall they preach, except they be sent? as it is written, How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace, and bring glad tidings of good things!
Act 13:3
And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away.
Mat 9:38
Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.
Isa 6:8
Also I heard the voice of the Lord, saying, Whom shall I send, and who will go for us? Then said I, Here am I; send me.
corruption_summary: One of the Genevan pastors sent into France, from a city that trained far more ministers than it kept.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a congregational arithmetic that counts its own pulpits and stops: a church trains for its vacancies and regards the sending of its best men elsewhere as a loss. Geneva trained for a kingdom it did not live in and gave its men away at a rate that would have emptied any ordinary presbytery.

The principle to recover is that sending is the Lord's own method and must be asked for. “Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest” (Mat 9:38). The church at Antioch laid hands on its two best teachers and let them go: “And when they had fasted and prayed, and laid their hands on them, they sent them away” (Act 13:3). The necessity is Paul's — “how shall they preach, except they be sent?” (Rom 10:15) — and the answer required is Isaiah's: “Here am I; send me” (Isa 6:8).

pos: n. (Pierre Merlin, c. 1535–1603, Huguenot pastor, chaplain to Coligny, survivor of the massacre of 1572)
etymology: French Pierre from Greek Petros, a stone; Merlin, from Old French, a small hawk.
biblical_def: Pierre Merlin was chaplain to Admiral Gaspard de Coligny, and he was in the Admiral's house in Paris on the night of the twenty-fourth of August 1572 when the killing began. Coligny was murdered in his bedroom and thrown into the street; Merlin hid in a hayloft for some days and got out of the city alive. He afterwards served at La Rochelle and at Nimes, presided at national synods, and lived another thirty years in the ministry. The dictionary records the hayloft. Saint Bartholomew's day killed thousands of French Protestants in Paris and the provinces, and it shaped the Huguenot mind permanently: after 1572 the French Reformed churches never again trusted a royal promise without a fortified town to stand behind it. Merlin is the man who saw it at the centre and then spent three decades doing the ordinary work of synods and pulpits, which is its own kind of answer to a massacre.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines massacre as the murder of numbers with cruelty, and chaplain as a clergyman who officiates in a family or army.
webster_full: MAS'SACRE, n. The murder of an individual, or the slaughter of numbers, with circumstances of cruelty.
CHAP'LAIN, n. An ecclesiastic who has the care of a chapel; a clergyman who belongs to a ship of war, a regiment, or a family.
AD'MIRAL, n. A naval officer of the highest rank; the commander of a fleet.
SYN'OD, n. An ecclesiastical council; a meeting of ministers and elders.
scriptures: If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us:
Psa 79:2
The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven, the flesh of thy saints unto the beasts of the earth.
Rev 6:10
And they cried with a loud voice, saying, How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood on them that dwell on the earth?
Psa 56:8
Thou tellest my wanderings: put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?
corruption_summary: He survived Saint Bartholomew's night in a hayloft and gave thirty more years to synods and pulpits.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a flattening of massacre into general human tragedy, which spares everyone the question of who ordered it and why. The dictionary names it: French Protestants were killed in their houses in Paris and in a dozen provincial cities in August and September 1572, with the connivance of the crown, because they were Protestants.

The principle to recover is that God records such blood and that His people are permitted to say so to Him. “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us” (Psa 124:2) is the psalm a survivor sings. The lament is unsparing: “The dead bodies of thy servants have they given to be meat unto the fowls of the heaven” (Psa 79:2). Under the altar the cry is for judgment and is not rebuked: “How long, O Lord, holy and true, dost thou not judge and avenge our blood” (Rev 6:10). And nothing is lost in the accounting — “put thou my tears into thy bottle: are they not in thy book?” (Psa 56:8).

pos: n. (Jean de Serres, c. 1540–1598, Huguenot pastor and historian of the French religious wars)
etymology: French Jean from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; de Serres, of the greenhouses or terraced slopes.
biblical_def: Jean de Serres was a Huguenot minister and schoolmaster of the Languedoc who became the principal contemporary historian of the French wars of religion, publishing a running Latin commentary on the state of religion and the commonwealth in France which was translated and read across Europe, and afterward a general history of France. He also served as a royal historiographer under Henry IV, and he wrote in favour of reconciling the confessions, which earned him suspicion from his own side. The dictionary records both the work and the hazard. A Protestant writing the history of a war he had lived through, for readers in England, Germany and the Netherlands who would form their politics by it, was handling something more dangerous than a pulpit. His record is partisan and it is also indispensable, and the dictionary says so plainly rather than pretending that a Huguenot account of the massacres is neutral. Scripture itself gives history written by participants with a declared interest in the outcome.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines history as a narration of facts and events, and annals as a history digested in order of time.
webster_full: HIS'TORY, n. An account of facts, particularly of facts respecting nations or states; a narration of events in the order of time.
AN'NALS, n. A history digested in the order of time; a relation of events in chronological order.
HISTORIOG'RAPHER, n. A historian; a writer of history; particularly, one appointed to record events.
COM'MENTARY, n. A historical narrative; a memoir of particular transactions.
scriptures: This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD.
Psa 44:1
To the chief Musician for the sons of Korah, Maschil. We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old.
Psa 78:6
That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children:
And the LORD said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.
corruption_summary: He wrote the contemporary history of the French wars for Protestant Europe, partisan and indispensable.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs in two directions at once. One is the demand that history be written from nowhere, by a man with no stake, which produces either paralysis or dishonesty. The other is the assumption that because every historian has a position, all accounts are equally reliable. De Serres had a position and also had facts, and his book is to be used the way Scripture teaches history to be used: tested, compared, and received where it is true.

The principle to recover is that God commands the recording of His works for the generations that have not seen them. “This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the LORD” (Psa 102:18). The fathers' telling is the ordinary channel: “We have heard with our ears, O God, our fathers have told us, what work thou didst in their days, in the times of old” (Psa 44:1). And the command to Moses is explicit about writing it down: “Write this for a memorial in a book” (Exo 17:14).

pos: n. (Michel Le Faucheur, c. 1585–1657, Huguenot pastor at Montpellier and Charenton, writer on the delivery of sermons)
etymology: French Michel from Hebrew Mikael, who is like God; Le Faucheur, the mower, the reaper.
biblical_def: Michel Le Faucheur pastored at Montpellier and then at Charenton, the great Reformed church that served Paris from outside the walls because Protestant worship was forbidden within them. He was reckoned among the finest preachers of the French church, and he left a short treatise on the delivery of a discourse — on voice, pace, carriage and gesture — which was translated into English and used for over a century by men who had never heard of him. The dictionary takes the treatise seriously and sets its limit. Le Faucheur's point was not that eloquence persuades; it was that a mumbled, hurried or affected delivery puts an obstacle between a congregation and the text, and that removing obstacles is part of a preacher's duty. He was writing for men who had one hour a week with people who had walked miles to get there. What he refused, and what Paul refused before him, was the substitution of performance for demonstration of the Spirit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines elocution as the mode of utterance or delivery, and gesture as motion of the body or limbs in speaking.
webster_full: ELOCU'TION, n. The mode of utterance or delivery of words, particularly in public discourses and arguments.
GES'TURE, n. A motion of the body or limbs, expressive of sentiment or passion; action in speaking.
PRONUNCIA'TION, n. The act of uttering with articulate sounds; the mode of uttering words or sentences.
DELIV'ERY, n. Utterance; pronunciation; manner of speaking.
scriptures: And my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power:
For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.
So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air.
Neh 8:8
So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
corruption_summary: He wrote on sermon delivery as the removal of obstacles, not as persuasion by performance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a pair of opposite errors. One treats the pulpit as a stage and makes delivery the point; the other treats any attention to delivery as carnal, and so excuses mumbling and self-indulgence as plainness. Le Faucheur's whole argument is that manner is a servant: it exists to get out of the way.

The principle to recover is that preaching works by the Spirit through an intelligible word. Paul disclaims the first error outright: “my speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of man's wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power” (1Co 2:4). He also disclaims self-display: “For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord” (2Co 4:5). And the second error is answered by the plain requirement of being understood — “except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken?” (1Co 14:9).

pos: n. (Charles Drelincourt, 1595–1669, pastor at Charenton and author of the Huguenot book on dying)
etymology: Germanic Karl, a free man; French Drelincourt, a place-name surname of Picardy.
biblical_def: Charles Drelincourt served the Reformed church at Charenton for forty-nine years and wrote the book that Huguenot families kept beside their Bibles: the Consolations of the Faithful Soul against the Fears of Death, which went through edition after edition in French, was translated into English, Dutch and German, and was still being reprinted a century and a half later. He also wrote catechisms, a dialogue for instructing children, and controversial works against Rome. The dictionary names the book on dying as his great work and the reason the entry exists. He wrote it for a people who had reason to expect violent death, and he did not meet their fear with distraction or with stoicism. He met it with the doctrine of the union of the believer with Christ, the certainty of the resurrection, and the plain statement that the sting has been taken out of death by someone else's dying. Three hundred years of Protestant deathbeds were steadied by that book.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines consolation as comfort and alleviation of distress of mind, and mortality as the state of being subject to death.
webster_full: CONSOLA'TION, n. Comfort; alleviation of misery, or refreshment of spirit; that which comforts.
MORTAL'ITY, n. Subjection to death or the necessity of dying; death.
STING, n. A sharp-pointed weapon; anything that gives acute pain.
RESURREC'TION, n. A rising again; the revival of the dead of the human race.
scriptures: O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?
Heb 2:15
And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage.
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live:
We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
corruption_summary: His Consolations against the Fears of Death steadied Protestant deathbeds for three centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern management of death by avoidance — the hospital word, the postponed conversation, the celebration of a life that declines to mention the judgment. Drelincourt's readers could not avoid the subject, and his book is accordingly direct: it tells a dying Christian what is true and why he may be confident, instead of promising that he will not mind.

The principle to recover is that Christ has defeated death and freed His people from the fear of it. “O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?” (1Co 15:55). The deliverance is named as a purpose of the incarnation: to “deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage” (Heb 2:15). The ground is a person, not a technique: “I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live” (Joh 11:25). And the prospect is stated as preference — “willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8).

pos: n. (Jean Mestrezat, 1592–1657, pastor at Charenton and controversialist against Rome)
etymology: French Jean from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Mestrezat, a Genevan family surname.
biblical_def: Jean Mestrezat was born at Geneva, came to Paris, and spent his ministry at Charenton, where he was the most formidable controversialist the French Reformed church possessed in the years when Cardinal Richelieu was systematically dismantling its political securities. He wrote on the Supper, on the authority of the church and of Scripture, and against the Roman doctrine of the mass; he debated in person; and he preached a long expository course on the Epistle to the Hebrews. Richelieu is said to have remarked that Mestrezat was the hardest of the Huguenot ministers to answer. The dictionary records him as a reminder of what the French church was losing and how. After La Rochelle fell in 1628 the Huguenots had no fortified towns and no army; what they still had was pulpits and presses, and the crown spent the next fifty-seven years closing those too, until the Edict of Nantes was revoked in 1685. Mestrezat spent his life on the one weapon that remained lawful.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines controversy as a disputation on a point of doctrine, and refute as to disprove and overthrow by argument.
webster_full: CON'TROVERSY, n. Dispute; debate; agitation of contrary opinions; a disputation on a point of doctrine.
REFU'TE, v.t. To disprove and overthrow by argument, evidence or countervailing proof.
DISPUTA'TION, n. The act of disputing; a reasoning or argumentation in opposition to another.
MASS, n. The service of the Romish church at the celebration of the eucharist.
scriptures: For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
corruption_summary: The hardest Huguenot minister to answer, spending his life on the one weapon left after La Rochelle fell.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the sacrifice of the mass, which Mestrezat answered from the Epistle to the Hebrews. Rome teaches that in the mass the one sacrifice of Christ is re-presented and offered for the living and the dead by a priest at an altar. The Scriptures teach that the offering was made once, by Christ Himself, and that He then sat down, which is what a priest with unfinished work cannot do. The modern ecumenical habit is to call this a difference of emphasis. It is a difference about whether the atonement is finished.

The standard is the text Mestrezat preached through. “But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God” (Heb 10:12). The method is apostolic: Apollos “mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ” (Act 18:28). The elder is required to be able to do it — “by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9) — and the weapons are not political: “For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4).

pos: n. (Raymond Gaches, 1615–1668, pastor at Charenton in the last generation before the Revocation)
etymology: Germanic Raginmund, counsel-protection; French Gaches, a surname of the Languedoc.
biblical_def: Raymond Gaches came from Castres in the Languedoc to the pulpit at Charenton, where he preached to the largest Reformed congregation in France in the reign of Louis XIV. His sermons were admired well beyond his own communion; he was known for a plain, affecting manner and for pressing the conscience rather than scoring points. He died in 1668, seventeen years before the Edict of Nantes was revoked. The dictionary places him last in this batch for that reason. Gaches preached to a church that still had a famous pulpit, a printing trade and a public standing, and which was gone within a generation: in 1685 the temple at Charenton was pulled down, the ministers were given a fortnight to leave the kingdom, and some two hundred thousand French Protestants went into exile. He did not know he was preaching to the last generation. No preacher does, and that is an argument for preaching as if he were.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines revocation as the act of recalling or annulling, and temple as a public edifice erected for worship.
webster_full: REVOCA'TION, n. The act of recalling or annulling; repeal; as the revocation of an edict.
TEM'PLE, n. A public edifice erected in honour of some deity; among the French Protestants, a place of worship.
EX'ODUS, n. Departure from a place; the second book of the Pentateuch.
REF'UGEE, n. One who flees to a place of safety; one who in times of persecution flees to a foreign country.

Joh 9:4
I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work.
Ecc 11:6
In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand: for thou knowest not whether shall prosper, either this or that, or whether they both shall be alike good.
Wherefore I take you to record this day, that I am pure from the blood of all men.
corruption_summary: He preached to the largest Reformed congregation in France, seventeen years before it was destroyed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the assumption of continuance — the quiet confidence that a congregation with a building, a reputation and a budget will be there in twenty years, which makes a preacher economical with his urgency. Charenton had all three in 1668 and was rubble in 1685.

The principle to recover is that the time to preach is now, because the night comes. “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season” (2Ti 4:2). Our Lord's own reckoning is temporal: “I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work” (Joh 9:4). The sower is told to sow without waiting for certainty: “In the morning sow thy seed, and in the evening withhold not thine hand” (Ecc 11:6). And the minister who has spoken plainly can say what Paul said — “I am pure from the blood of all men” (Act 20:26).
